summary.text:
A tidy Q3 update that reconciles cleanly. Our PWLB file holds five loans totalling £107.60m at a weighted 2.534%, matching Table 14 exactly and the 2.5% Table 3 rounds to. The balance sheet identity closes both years — 840.0 − 311.8 − 303.5 = 224.7 for 2024/25 actual, and the 2025/26 forecast closes to 271.4 against the printed 271.3 (£0.1m rounding). All prudential and treasury indicators comply.

The interesting thing in this paper is Table 15. £25m LOBO called in the first half at a proposed rate of 7.23%, repaid at no cost from cash. Almost no council prints the rate the lender actually asked — of some 200 treasury reports we now hold, the only others that do are Oldham (7.67% and 6.70%), Wolverhampton (6.19%, 6.21%, 6.26%) and Reading (a Dexia LOBO called at 6.26% in January). Seven data points across four councils, refused in every case, in a 6.19%-to-7.67% band. That is a picture no individual authority can assemble from its own papers.

The remaining LOBO book is £163m in nine loans (eight at 4.75%, one at 4.63%), and the maturity table puts £52.6m of borrowing into the sub-two-year buckets — since all PWLBs mature 2056-2068, that £52.6m is entirely LOBO call exposure bucketed by next call date. Paragraph 7.11 flagged a further £6m call date 'towards the end of this financial year', which by our reading date (16 August 2026) has passed; the outcome will sit in the Q4 outturn or Q1 26/27 report we do not hold.

Two other things worth noting. The investment book runs a weighted average maturity of 23 days against 7 days for the Arlingclose 'Similar LAs' peer group and 13 days for all LAs — materially longer than peers, at slightly higher yield (4.07% vs 3.96%) and lower bail-in exposure (51% vs 83%). And the liability benchmark shows existing borrowing at £276.8m held flat against a benchmark rising to £409.9m by 2028 — a £133m borrowing gap opening in about two years on the council's own forecast. On today's curve the PWLB book prices about £49.6m below par (indicative only).

NO OFFICER EMAIL published anywhere. Contact officers named on p.22 are Tony Thompstone (Strategic Finance Manager, 0161 793 2016) and May Sung (Finance Manager, 0161 793 2851). The S151 is referred to only as 'the Chief Finance Officer' in 6.3 and is unnamed in this paper.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Q3 update that went to Overview and Scrutiny Board on 4 March, offered ahead of the next treasury item. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report reconciles cleanly, so this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

A cross-check first. We hold five PWLB loans for you totalling £107.60m at a weighted 2.534%, which is your Table 14 exactly and the 2.5% you round to in Table 3. Your balance sheet closes both years — General Fund CFR £840.0m less £303.5m of other long-term liabilities less £311.8m of external borrowing is the £224.7m of internal borrowing you print at 31 March 2025, and the 2025/26 forecast closes to £271.4m against your £271.3m (£0.1m rounding).

We wrote because of your Table 15. £25m LOBO called in the first half at a proposed 7.23%, repaid at no cost from cash. Almost no council prints the rate the lender actually asked. Of the treasury reports we've read the only others that do are Oldham (7.67% and 6.70%), Wolverhampton (6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26%) and Reading (a Dexia LOBO called at 6.26% in January and repaid within the week). Seven data points across four councils, refused in every case, in a 6.19%-to-7.67% band — yours is the second-highest we hold, below only Oldham's 7.67%. That is the only hard evidence in the sector of what LOBO lenders are actually pricing options at, and no single authority can assemble it from its own papers.

Your remaining £163m LOBO book carries call dates that put £52.6m into the sub-two-year buckets in your Table 12 — since your PWLBs all mature 2056 to 2068, that £52.6m is entirely LOBO call exposure. Your paragraph 7.11 flagged a further £6m LOBO with a call date towards the end of the last financial year, which by now has passed. Whether each subsequent call ends the same way as Loan 1 is a decision taken against the market on the day, and today's certainty curve on notice 314/26 is 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five and 6.38% at twenty.

Two other things. Your Table 17 puts weighted average maturity on investments at 23 days against 7 for the 'Similar LAs' peer group and 13 for all LAs — materially longer than peers, at slightly higher yield and 51% bail-in exposure versus 83%. Distinctive shape rather than a concern. And your Table 10 shows existing borrowing at £276.8m held flat against a benchmark rising to £409.9m by 2028 — a £133m gap opening in about two years on your own forecast. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis alongside a daily read of the discount position on your PWLB book; on today's curve it prices about £49.6m below par, but that is indicative only — the DMO's quote is the binding one, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, four fit Salford. LOBO loans, for the calls still ahead. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, for the £133m opening question. Break costs and premature repayment, given the shape of your PWLB book. And Local Authority credit analysis, for the investment counterparty side. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
